title: TAC: Timestamped Audio Captioning
claim: Given only raw input, our model outputs structured, time-grounded descriptions that cleanly separate overlapping events in a complex scene.
layout: Single stacked panel: frames, spectrogram, colored lanes, then color-matched caption text
description: A single wide figure stacked vertically. At the top is a strip of five video frames from a fantasy scene: a burning castle, a green monster, a black gap, a caped figure in front of a tower, and a figure in a dark forest. Below is a purple-orange spectrogram of the audio. Under that are colored horizontal lanes in blue, red, green, orange, purple and cyan. Each lane marks the time span of one sound event, and some lanes overlap. At the bottom, the text 'Audio → TAC →' leads into a paragraph of timestamped captions such as '[music] Heroic brass fanfares… from 0.0s to 3.8s'. Each caption is colored to match its lane. The eye goes first to the colorful lanes and then to the large colored text.
caption: Given only audio, \method{} generates structured, timestamped descriptions of overlapping sound events. We visualize the timestamps produced by \method{} as temporal lanes above. Colors indicate correspondence between text and temporal lanes.
abstract: Large Audio Language Models struggle to disentangle overlapping events in complex acoustic scenes, yielding temporally inconsistent captions and frequent hallucinations. We introduce Timestamped Audio Captioner (TAC), a model that produces temporally grounded audio descriptions at varying degrees of detail and resolution. TAC is trained with a synthetic data pipeline that constructs challenging and dynamic mixtures from real-world audio sources, enabling robust learning under realistic polyphonic conditions. Across event detection and dense captioning, TAC outperforms all competing methods, with a low hallucination rate and accurate temporal grounding. We also introduce TAC-V, an audio-visual pipeline to generate semantically rich audio-visual descriptions. We then show that TAC and TAC-V serves as a "semantic bridge" for a text-only reasoner: a simple TAC$\rightarrow$LLM and TAC-V$\rightarrow$LLM cascade achieves state-of-the-art scores on benchmarks for both audio (MMAU-Pro, MMSU, MMAR) and audio-visual (DailyOmni, VideoHolmes) understanding and reasoning respectively.
